t: #3862 Find the Smallest Balanced Index — Prefix Sums with a Capped Suffix Product
o: We scan for the smallest index i where the sum of everything before i equals the product of everything after i (empty left sum = 0, empty right product = 1). In Example 1 ([2,1,2]) index 1 has left sum 2 and right product 2, so the answer is 1. In Example 3 ([1]) index 0 has left sum 0 vs right product 1, so the answer is -1. With n up to 1e5, recomputing products naively is O(n^2) and too slow, so we precompute prefix sums and suffix products. The catch: products overflow 64-bit integers quickly, but since every element is >= 1, once the running product exceeds the maximum possible sum (about 1e14) it can never match again — so we clamp it.
k: Prefix sums from the left and suffix products from the right let us test every index in O(1).
Because all values are >= 1, clamping the product at anything above the maximum achievable sum (n * 1e9 <= 1e14) keeps arithmetic in 64-bit range while preserving equality checks.

a.n: Approach 1: Prefix Sum + Clamped Suffix Product
a.i: Build prefix[i] = sum of nums[0..i-1] and suf[i] = product of nums[i..n-1], clamping the product once it exceeds a cap larger than any possible sum. Index i is balanced iff prefix[i] == suf[i+1]; return the first such i.
s: Compute prefix sums left to right.
Compute suffix products right to left, clamping at CAP = 2e14.
Scan i from 0 to n-1 and return the first i with prefix[i] == suf[i+1], else -1.
a.t: O(n) — three linear passes over the array.
a.sp: O(n) — two auxiliary arrays of size n+1.

a.i: For each candidate index, directly sum the left part and multiply the right part. Simple and obviously correct, but quadratic — acceptable only for tiny inputs.
s: For each i from 0 to n-1, compute the left sum and right product from scratch.
Return the first balanced index, else -1.
a.t: O(n^2) in the worst case — nested loops per index.

w: Use the prefix/suffix approach in an interview; mention the clamping trick explicitly since raw products overflow everywhere except Python. Pitfalls: forgetting the empty-side conventions (left sum 0, right product 1), and overflowing 64-bit products in C++/Java/JS. Follow-ups: what if negative numbers were allowed (clamping breaks — use big integers or hashing), or if you needed all balanced indices instead of the smallest.
